title: PagerDuty Datadog Integration: Setup Guide (2026)
summary: A PagerDuty Datadog integration routes Datadog alerts to PagerDuty incidents and sends events back. Build it in an afternoon using a no-code tool.
body_markdown:
## Build PagerDuty Datadog integration fast


### How an alert becomes an incident


A monitor evaluates a metric on a schedule and changes state. On a state change it notifies a destination, and for paging that destination is an events endpoint that takes a routing key tied to one service.


The service's escalation policy decides who is paged, and a deduplication key decides whether the message opens a new incident or updates an open one.


The reverse direction is a webhook. The incident system posts a message on each lifecycle change, and something on the receiving end turns it into a log line, an annotation or a mute.


### Four ways to connect PagerDuty and Datadog


The vendors' native integration is simplest, and it is enough when an alert should just page the on-call. A workflow tool sits in the middle when you need routing, enrichment or a chat notice.


A small script or serverless function that receives the webhook and calls the REST APIs gives full control, at the price of code you must maintain. Infrastructure-as-code, such as Terraform, suits teams that want monitors and services defined in version control.


The choice turns on who will maintain it, not on what is possible.


### What teams actually automate between the two


Most teams automate one of three jobs, **which means two remain manual** . The first is paging: a Datadog monitor goes critical and the right PagerDuty service opens an incident.


> The choice turns on who will maintain it, not on what is possible.


The second is enrichment, where a new incident gets context from Datadog, such as the monitor's query or a link to the dashboard, so the on-call engineer isn't hunting for it at 3 a.m.


The third job is cleanup: when an incident resolves in PagerDuty, the Datadog monitor is muted or annotated so the alert doesn't keep firing.


Pick one. A workflow that tries all three is hard to debug, and you won't know which step produced the duplicate page.


### Requirements for the PagerDuty Datadog integration


Gather these first; missing keys are the most common reason a first run fails.


- An account with the workflow tool
- A PagerDuty API key
- A Datadog API key and application key, plus the Datadog site your organization uses
- One chosen job to automate


A key from one site is rejected by another, and the failure looks like a bad key rather than a wrong address. That is why the Datadog site matters: keys are issued per site.


### The fastest path, and where the native integration stops


To get there fastest, build the workflow in[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) . PagerDuty and Datadog are both among its 750 integrations, counted from the open source monorepo, so the trigger from one app and the action in the other come from lists you can read.


Start from the single job you chose and run it with a test alert before you add anything else.


When your job needs an endpoint that isn't listed, such as a Datadog call the integration doesn't expose, don't guess at a field name or hope a setting exists. The native integrations only cover the triggers and actions they list.


Add an HTTP request step or a webhook step and call the vendor's API directly, using the same keys you gathered above. That keeps the workflow no-code and avoids debugging a feature that was never there.
